Case report
A 14-year-old girl with hyperekplexia having GLRB mutations
Jun Mine a,⇑, Takeshi Taketani a,b, Shusuke Otsubo c, Kazuko Kishi a, Seiji Yamaguchi a
a Department of Pediatrics, Shimane University School of Medicine, Japan
b Division of Blood Transfusion, Shimane University Hospital, Japan
c Otsubo Kodomo Clinic, Japan
Received 27 July 2012; received in revised form 23 October 2012; accepted 24 October 2012
Abstract
Hyperekplexia manifests as generalized stiﬀness and an excessive startle reﬂex to stimuli. It starts in the neonatal period and is
transmitted in many cases via autosomal dominant inheritance. The etiology is an abnormality of the glycinergic neurotransmission
system that is involved in inhibitory neurotransmission. Aberrations of ﬁve genes related to this neurotransmission system have been
identiﬁed. The patient was a 14-year-old girl with mild mental retardation. None of her family members had a neuromuscular dis-
ease. An excessive startle reﬂex and generalized stiﬀness were noted immediately after birth and she was diagnosed with epilepsy
because epileptic discharges were observed. However, the disease was resistant to various antiepileptic drugs and the startle
responses persisted. GLRB gene mutations (R50X/Q216fsx222) were identiﬁed, after which the patient was diagnosed with hyper-
ekplexia. The startle reﬂex improved when clonazepam treatment was initiated. When patients have a persistent startle reﬂex, it is
necessary to consider hyperekplexia, even if epileptic discharges are observed. Only four cases with GLRB mutations, including the
present patient, have been reported. To make a deﬁnite diagnosis of hyperekplexia, it may be useful to screen for genes that are
involved in the glycinergic neurotransmission system.

Keywords: Hyperekplexia; GLRB; Startle disease; Nose-tapping test; Reﬂex epilepsy
1. Introduction
Hyperekplexia starts in the neonatal period and man-
ifests as generalized stiﬀness and an excessive startle
reﬂex to stimuli [1]. There are no abnormalities in blood
tests, urinalysis, imaging studies such as computed
tomography and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI),
or physiological examinations including electroencepha-
lography (EEG) and electromyography. Consequently,
the nose-tapping test (head-retraction reﬂex) is an
important test that is used to diagnose hyperekplexia
[1]. Umbilical hernia, hip joint dislocation, sudden
infant death syndrome, epilepsy, and transient delayed
motor development are known complications [1]. The
symptoms improve with aging but startle response-asso-
ciated severe trauma and death may occur unless appro-
priate treatment or instruction is given [1–2]. However,
the awareness of this disease is low, and unnecessary
tests and treatments are performed in many cases
because of misdiagnosis of epilepsy or anxiety syn-
drome. Regarding treatment, many reports have indi-
cated that clonazepam (CZP) is eﬀective [1–6].
This disease is thought to be caused by abnormalities
in the glycinergic neurotransmission system, which is
involved in inhibitory neurotransmission [1–6]. Muta-
tions in ﬁve glycinergic neurotransmission system genes
have been identiﬁed in patients with hyperekplexia,
namely genes encoding the a1 subunit of the glycine
receptor ( GLRA1), the glycine transporter 2 ( SLC6A5),

the b-subunit of the human inhibitory glycine receptor
(GLRB), the gephyrin gene ( GPHN), and the collybistin
gene (ARHGEF9). Aberrations of these genes have been
noted in 80% of hyperekplexia cases and, consequently,
tests identifying these mutations play a very important
role when deﬁnitively diagnosing this disease [2].
However, only three cases with GLRB mutations have
been reported [3–5]. Herein, we report the case of a
14-year-old girl with hyperekplexia who had novel
GLRB mutations.
2. Case report
A girl was born at 40 weeks of gestation with a birth
weight of 3190 g. No abnormalities such as asphyxia
were noted in the perinatal period. She did not have
umbilical hernia or hip joint dislocations. There was
no familial history that was suggestive of startle
responses. A history of epilepsy, and neurological or
mental disorder, was also absent. Hypertonia appeared
immediately after birth and generalized stiﬀness accom-
panied by cyanosis was noted. Blood test, imaging, and
EEG results were normal. Retroﬂexion of the neck in
response to hitting the philtrum with a ﬁnger, namely,
the nose-tapping test, was noted. However, hyperekplex-
ia was not diagnosed at this point. Instead, the patient
was diagnosed with epilepsy. Antiepileptics, such as phe-
nobarbital, phenytoin, and zonisamide, were adminis-
tered but the startle responses did not improve.
During her infancy, the patient could not land on her
hands when she fell down and, consequently, she injured
herself repeatedly. Her developmental milestones, such
as head control, sitting, crawling, and gait were normal
in early infancy. While, at 4 years and 4 months of age,
her developmental quotient scores, assessed by the
Enjoji scale of infant analytical development, for
movement, speech, and interpersonal skills/language
comprehension were 81, 69, and 50, respectively, which
indicated a mild delay. However, the patient had no
problems in terms of normal living activities and was
in a regular class after entering school. Repeated blood
tests and brain MRIs during the course of the child’s life
did not detect any abnormalities. At 12 years of age, an
EEG performed during intermission revealed a localized
spike and waves in the left occipital region ( Fig. 1 ). The
patient never had any seizures apart from the startle
response.
Genetic analysis for hyperekplexia was sought and
approved by the ethical committee in the Shimane
University School of Medicine.
After obtaining written consent from the parents,
DNA was extracted from the peripheral blood of the
patient and genes involved in the glycinergic neurotrans-
mission system were analyzed by PCR and direct
sequencing. Aberrations in the GLRA1 or SLC6A5
genes were not observed but a compound heterozygote
mutation was detected in the GLRB gene ( Fig. 2 ). In
one allele, there was a nonsense mutation, where TGA
substituted the arginine-encoding CGA codon at posi-
tion 50. In the other allele, four bases, including three
bases encoding glutamine at position 216, were deleted,
thus causing a frame-shift. A similar frame-shift was
noted in one allele of her mother but her father did
not have any mutations in the GLRB gene. The patient
and her family underwent genetic counseling by the
medical doctor certiﬁed as a clinical geneticist, both
before and after the genetic analysis.
At 14 years of age, the patient still fell down when
general rigidity was induced. She was startled by the
sound of a closing shoji (a sliding paper door), or

sneezed by herself. Occasionally, these falls resulted in
injuries that would require sutures. After the GLRB
mutation was identiﬁed and hyperekplexia was diag-
nosed, the antiepileptics were withdrawn and CZP
administration was initiated. This resolved the startle
responses.
3. Discussion
Aberrations in ﬁve genes relating to the glycinergic
neurotransmission system that is involved in inhibitory
neurotransmission have been identiﬁed in hyperekplexia
[1–8]. The GLRA1 gene encodes glycine receptor subunit
a [2], while GPHN, ARHGEF9,a n d SLC6A5 encode
gephyrin [6], collybistin [7], and the glycine transporter
GlyT2 [8], respectively. Gephyrin and collybistin are
proteins that cause the clustering of the glycine receptor

seen in the left occipital region.

[2], while the glycine transporter is a presynaptic NaCl-
dependent transporter [2]. The GLRB gene, which was
mutated in our patient, encodes glycine receptor subunit
b [3]. It is believed that when gene aberration occurs in
one or more of these ﬁve genes, normal glycine transmis-
sion is impaired and the inhibitory neurotransmission
pathway is inhibited. This results in the dominance of
the excitatory transmission system, which induces the
symptoms of hyperekplexia. CZP is an eﬀective drug
for hyperekplexia because it promotes the action of
GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter. GABA and
the glycine receptor are widespread in the same regions
of the central nervous system and the drug is thought to
improve startle symptoms by promoting GABA activity,
thereby enhancing glycine receptor reactivity [1–3,7–8].
Only three cases (one case was of a large family) with
GLRB mutations have been reported previously [3–5].
Most of the patients with GLRB mutations exhibited
generalized stiﬀness at birth and had excessive startle
responses to stimuli; they also responded favorably to
CZP. In two cases, the GLRB mutations were compound
heterozygous mutations: one was IVS5 + 5G ! A/
p.S343F and the other was IVS5 + 5G ! A/p.G229D.
In the large family case, the GLRB mutation was a
homozygous mutation (p.M177R). Except for her
abnormal EEG results at age 12, the course of our
patient was consistent with those of the other patients
with GLRB mutations. Moreover, a compound hetero-
zygous mutation (p.R50X/p.Q216fsx222) was found in
our case. These observations suggest that mutations in
GLRB can cause hyperekplexia and that patients with
GLRB mutations have the same clinical features as
patients with mutations in other genes that participate
in glycinergic neurotransmission.
Diseases that should be diﬀerentiated from hyperekp-
lexia include reﬂex epilepsy [1,9]. Hyperekplexia and
reﬂex epilepsy share two common features, namely,
the startle response and poor responsiveness to various
antiepileptic drugs [9]. Reﬂex epilepsy is distinguished
from hyperekplexia by the presence of interictal EEG
abnormalities. While our patient exhibited an abnormal
interictal EEG at age 12, we believe that this EEG
abnormality was not related to the GLRB mutations
of the patient for two reasons. First, the other patients
with hyperekplexia who had mutations in the GLRA
or GLRB genes generally had normal interictal EEG.
Second, the EEG abnormality in our patient remained
after her startle responses were resolved by CZP. Never-
theless, the EEG abnormality of our patient made it dif-
ﬁcult to diﬀerentiate between reﬂex epilepsy and
hyperekplexia. Although the usefulness of combined
ictal EEG is reported to distinguish epilepsy and hyper-
ekplexia [10], generally, it would be diﬃcult to distin-
guish them by ictal EEG. Therefore, this case suggests
that to make a deﬁnite diagnosis of hyperekplexia, it
may be useful to analyze genes involved in the glyciner-
gic neurotransmission system. These analyses will aid
the correct diagnosis of patients who have features of
hyperekplexia, such as generalized stiﬀness that includes
limb rigidity and a negative Moro reﬂex, an excessive
startle reﬂex when subjected to unexpected stimuli, a
positive nose-tapping test, and comorbidities such as
Fig. 2. The GLRB mutations that were identiﬁed in the patient. One allele had a nonsense mutation where TGA had substituted the arginine-

encoding CGA codon at position 50. The other allele had lost four bases, including the three bases that encoded glutamine at position 216. This
deletion caused a frame-shift.

umbilical hernia, hip joint dislocations, and epilepsy.
Testing for mutations will be particularly useful if the
startle responses of the patients continue despite the
administration of antiepileptic drugs.
